title: The standing prayer
hookLine: Ardas is prayed standing, hands folded, at the start and end of everything

cards: At the end of a gurdwara service, the whole room does the same thing. Everyone who was sitting cross-legged on the floor gets up. They stand, face the Guru Granth Sahib, and fold their hands in front of them.
One person starts speaking, steady and rhythmic, and every so often the whole room answers in one word: Waheguru.

You'll see the same thing at a wedding, before a new business opens, before a long journey, beside a hospital bed, at a funeral, before a meal is served from the langar, and after. It's the Sikh prayer for everything.

teach.b: It's called Ardas. Sikh tradition explains the word through the Persian arz-dasht: a petition, a written request, the kind handed up to a king.
Heard that way, the name says what the Ardas is: a petition to God, made standing, the way you'd stand before someone you honor. It isn't one of the hymns of the Guru Granth Sahib.

It grew up in the community, and its standard form is set out in the Sikh code of conduct, the Rehat Maryada. Over the coming weeks we'll go through it line by line. For now, here's the shape, in three movements.

teach.h: FIRST, IT OPENS WITH THE GURUS.
teach.b: First, it opens with lines from Guru Gobind Singh's Var Sri Bhagauti Ji Ki, remembering God's power and the Gurus by name.
Second, it remembers: the Guru Granth Sahib, the Panj Pyare, the Sahibzade, the martyrs, the gurdwaras, the long history of the community.

teach.h: LAST, IT ASKS, FOR TODAY TOO.
teach.b: Third, it asks: for the Name, for faith, for the good of the whole Khalsa, and then for whatever this particular moment needs, a wedding, a journey, a recovery. Then it closes by asking for the good of everyone.
Notice that order. Before asking for anything, the Ardas remembers.
By the time the request comes, you've been reminded who you stand with. And the room keeps answering, Waheguru, so the prayer is never one person's alone.
The opening and the remembering stay much the same everywhere; the ask at the end changes with the occasion. It carries the whole history of the community, and room for this one Tuesday.

how: Sikhs say the Ardas standing with folded hands, facing the Guru Granth Sahib where it is present, at the end of services and at the start and end of any important undertaking, with the sangat answering Waheguru.

games.q: you're in a gurdwara and the service ends. everyone around you gets up from the floor. what's happening?
o: the service is over and people are leaving.
the Ardas: everyone stands, hands folded, facing the Guru Granth Sahib.
games.why: the whole room stands for the Ardas and answers Waheguru together. it's said at the start and end of nearly everything.

practice: If you can, stand with your feet steady and your hands folded in front of you, and notice whether standing feels different from sitting, as if someone were in front of you.
If you pray, ask God for one thing you need today in your own plain words, and end with Waheguru. If you don't, name silently one thing you hope for, for yourself and for someone else.
